idiom_name: one &AppCtx parameter threaded through the call chain
implementation_notes: Rust's default is the neutral one: pass an explicit `&AppCtx` (or the specific dependencies) to the functions that need it, and let the borrow checker keep the relay honest. Ownership is the Rust twist - relayed state is borrowed (`&Ctx`) or shared behind an `Arc`, dangling-reference versions of the pattern do not compile, and grouping values into one context struct keeps signatures stable when the context grows. Keep explicit parameters for local dependencies; the relay is justified while it stays shallow.
pitfalls: Closures and spawned tasks that capture a reference to the context need a lifetime that outlives them; `Arc<Ctx>` fixes it but turns the relay into shared ownership that must be audited.
One `AppCtx` for everything becomes a god object: every function depends on the whole context; split it by capability as it grows.

variants.name: thread_local! ambient per-thread state
variants.implementation_notes: For genuinely per-thread infrastructure Rust's standard library offers `thread_local!` statics (stable since 1.0), which create a value per thread and expose it through a `LocalKey`, e.g. `STATE.with(|s| ...)`. It is the closest thing in std to ambient state, but it is not scoped consumption: thread pools reuse threads, so values leak between tasks; async tasks may migrate between threads, so the value is not visible where expected; and access requires a closure, which keeps the dependency visible. Use it for allocators, arenas and thread-bound caches, not for request data.
pitfalls: A `thread_local!` value belongs to the OS thread, not the async task: with a work-stealing executor a resumed task can observe another thread's state.
Thread-local destructors run at thread exit, so values holding resources can outlive the logical scope that created them.

variants.name: Reactive-framework context (Leptos/Dioxus)
variants.implementation_notes: Rust UI frameworks implement the context remedy themselves: in Leptos a value is bound with `provide_context(value)` on a reactive owner and read anywhere below with `use_context::<T>()`, mirroring React's provider/consumer split; Dioxus exposes the same shape. This is the idiomatic replacement inside a component tree and shows that the remedy is framework-level, while the non-UI answer stays explicit parameters plus a context struct.
pitfalls: Contexts in reactive frameworks are keyed by type: two values of the same type collide, so wrap them in newtypes or named keys.
The context is tied to the reactive owner: spawning work outside that owner (a detached task, a server fn) loses access to it.
